interviewQuestions.question: Why does p99 latency matter more than the average when evaluating a service's performance?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd start by pointing out what an average actually hides: it collapses an entire distribution into one number, so a handful of very slow requests barely move it if most requests are fast. p99 latency instead tells you what the slowest 1% of requests actually experienced -- the tail the average is specifically built to ignore.

The reason that tail matters is scale: at a service handling a million requests a day, the p99 isn't a rare edge case -- it's ten thousand requests, ten thousand real users, hitting that slow path *every single day*. A platform that only watches the average can look perfectly healthy on a dashboard while a meaningful, and often growing, slice of real users have a bad experience.

**Testing:** whether you understand that percentiles and averages measure fundamentally different things, and that at production scale the 'rare' tail case is a guaranteed daily occurrence rather than a statistical curiosity you can ignore.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why p99, not average

interviewQuestions.question: A team adds a `user_id` label to a request-count metric to debug a customer issue. Two days later, the monitoring backend starts falling over. What happened?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
This is the cardinality trap: adding a label whose value comes from an effectively unbounded set — a raw user ID, a full request path with dynamic segments, a UUID — multiplies the number of distinct stored time series, because most metrics backends store one time series per unique combination of metric name and label values, not per metric name alone. A metric like `requests_total{status="200"}` might have a handful of time series total across a small set of status codes, but `requests_total{status="200", user_id="..."}` creates a brand new time series for every single distinct user who's ever made a request — for a service with millions of users, that's potentially millions of new time series from one label addition, each consuming its own memory and storage in the backend.

The failure shows up with a delay, which is exactly why it's dangerous: the label addition itself deploys cleanly and looks fine immediately, but the time-series count keeps growing every day as more distinct users generate their first request, until the backend's memory or its cost budget is exhausted — by the time anyone notices, undoing it means finding and reverting the label change, then often waiting for the backend to actually reclaim or expire the now-useless high-cardinality series it already created.

The actual fix at instrumentation time is discipline about label values before they ship: label values must be drawn from a small, known, bounded set — status codes, HTTP methods, service names — never anything with effectively unbounded cardinality like a raw user ID or a full dynamic path. If per-user debugging is genuinely needed, that data belongs in structured logs or a trace, which are built to handle high-cardinality fields, not in a metric label, which structurally isn't.

**Testing:** whether you can explain why cardinality problems specifically show up with a delay and connect that to why they're dangerous, not just define cardinality as a term.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Debugging a cardinality explosion

interviewQuestions.question: When would you choose a push-based metrics model over Prometheus's pull-based one?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The deciding factor is whether the thing emitting metrics is reliably alive and reachable at the moment the backend would want to scrape it — pull assumes a long-running, discoverable target that's there to be scraped on a schedule; push doesn't need that assumption to hold at all. Prometheus's pull model fits a long-running service well specifically because the backend controls its own pacing — it scrapes each target's `/metrics` endpoint on its own interval, which means the backend, not every individual service, decides how much scrape load it can absorb, and a target that's temporarily slow to respond just delays that one scrape rather than overwhelming anything.

That assumption breaks down for short-lived or batch jobs: a job that runs for 30 seconds and exits might not exist anymore by the time a pull-based backend's next scheduled scrape would hit it, meaning its metrics simply never get collected under a pure pull model — there's no window in which "scrape it later" works, because later it's gone. A push model sidesteps this cleanly: the job actively sends its metrics to a collector before it exits, so the metric's lifetime doesn't depend on lining up with an external scrape schedule at all.

The trade-off going to push is that the collector now has to handle inbound load arriving from every source on its own schedule rather than pacing itself — a large fleet of short-lived jobs all pushing around the same time can spike the collector's ingest load in a way a pull-based backend, which paces its own scrapes, is structurally protected from. In practice, many real systems use both: pull for the long-running core services, and a push gateway specifically for ephemeral batch jobs that pull can't reach in time.

**Testing:** whether you can name the specific failure mode pull has with short-lived jobs, not just recite that push and pull are 'different collection models' without a concrete reason to pick one.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Push vs pull, and when push wins
